system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Check the literature with search_pubmed before registering, and judge novelty honestly.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker HOT_PIK3CA (PIK3CA hotspot mutation).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

content.text: Robust across lineages. Oncogene addiction to mutant PIK3CA (alpelisib) is well established. Registering PIK3CA, and AKT1 as a second, more exploratory candidate.

input.mechanism: Oncogene addiction: hotspot (E545K/H1047R) p110alpha drives constitutive PI3K-AKT signalling; mutant lines depend on the mutant allele (basis of alpelisib/inavolisib).
Downstream effector dependence: PIK3CA-mutant signalling channels through AKT1 (capivasertib efficacy in PIK3CA/AKT/PTEN-altered breast cancer).

input.summary: For PIK3CA hotspot-mutant lines, the clear top selective dependency is PIK3CA itself (oncogene addiction). In the discovery set, the effect was adjusted for lineage, and it held up in every lineage examined and when any one lineage was left out. It replicated strongly in held-out Broad lines (p=4e-13) and in Sanger screens (p=3e-24). This is well established and matches clinical use of alpelisib and inavolisib, the drugs that block mutant p110alpha. AKT1 was a weaker downstream candidate. It passed the threshold in Sanger screens (p=0.0014) but not in held-out Broad lines (p=0.044), so it did not replicate. No new partner gene other than PIK3CA came close to significance after correcting for multiple testing.

findings.claim: PIK3CA hotspot-mutant cancer cells depend selectively on PIK3CA itself (mean effect about -0.9 vs -0.4; 51 of 62 discovery lines strongly dependent), and this holds across lineages.
PIK3CA hotspot-mutant lines showed a modestly greater dependence on AKT1 that passed in Sanger screens but not in held-out Broad lines.
